historical_timeline.summary: Law degree from Columbia Law School.
Passport cancelled by the State Department; blacklisting and loss of income follow.
Prostate surgery and a first breakdown followed by deep depression.
Called before the House Un-American Activities Committee.
Suicide attempt in Moscow; illness ends his career.
Admitted to the Priory clinic in London; many electroconvulsive treatments.
Returns to the United States after hospital care in East Berlin.
Moves to Philadelphia to live with his sister.
Dies in Philadelphia of complications of a stroke.

claims.statement: Paul Leroy Robeson was born on April 9, 1898, in Princeton, New Jersey.
His father, the Rev. William Drew Robeson, was a minister, and his mother was Maria Louisa Bustill.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; his parents are given no role in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In 1915 he was awarded a four-year academic scholarship to Rutgers, where he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and graduated as valedictorian in 1919; he had been named to college All-America football teams.
In 1923 he earned a law degree from Columbia Law School.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a documented education fact only.

claims.statement: In 1950 the State Department cancelled his passport, saying his overseas travel was 'contrary to the best interests of the United States'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the sustained political persecution in the modern episode.

claims.statement: His passport was restored in 1958, after eight years, following a Supreme Court ruling in a similar case that the withdrawal of a passport violated a citizen's constitutionally protected liberty.

He was blacklisted: his concerts were cancelled, record companies stopped recording him, his name was struck from the All-America teams and newsreel footage of him was destroyed, and his yearly income fell from more than $150,000 to less than $3,000.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the loss of work and income in the modern social history.

claims.statement: In 1956 he was called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment and closed by saying, 'You gentlemen belong with the Alien and Sedition Acts, and you are the nonpatriots, and you are the un-Americans, and you ought to be ashamed of yourselves.'
His biographer Martin Duberman describes his first breakdown in 1955, after health problems related to prostate surgery: a period of intense, driven energy that was followed by a deep depression.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the recurrent depression; reported through a secondary account of the Duberman biography.

claims.statement: A writer reviewing the Duberman biography has argued that he had the classic symptoms of bipolar disorder; no formal diagnosis of bipolar disorder in his lifetime is quoted.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not adopted. The modern episode screens for bipolar disorder (MDQ and a structured interview) and records why it is not diagnosed.

claims.statement: In March 1961, in Moscow, he became acutely paranoid and suicidal and made a suicide attempt.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; no modern visit falls in this period.

claims.statement: From September 1961 he was treated at the Priory clinic in London for nearly two years, where he received a large number of electroconvulsive treatments, 54 by his son's later count, in five courses over about twenty months, together with heavy doses of drugs; reviewers of the Duberman biography note electroshock for recurrent depression and suicide attempts.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. Contrast for teaching: modern ECT is offered only after informed consent, given under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant, usually right unilateral with an ultrabrief pulse, in a defined course with cognitive testing before and during treatment; this record does not judge whether his treatment met the standards of its time.

claims.statement: He later spent time in a psychiatric hospital in East Berlin and returned to the United States in December 1963.
Illness ended his professional career in 1961.
His son, Paul Robeson Jr., believed that his father had been poisoned by United States intelligence with a mind-altering drug and that a doctor who treated him had links to the MK-Ultra program.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An allegation by a relative, reported as his belief; not confirmed by the cited sources and not adopted. The modern episode makes no claim about it.

claims.statement: Federal agencies kept files on him: the CIA opened a file in 1943, and the FBI kept a 'status of health' file on him between April and June 1961; his biographer drew on his FBI files.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports treating his concern about surveillance in the modern episode as realistic rather than delusional.

claims.statement: From 1966 he lived in Philadelphia under the care of his sister Marian until his death, and lived as a recluse.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; his sister is history only.

claims.statement: He died of complications of a stroke on January 23, 1976, in Philadelphia, at the age of 77.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize and treat recurrent severe major depression in a 58-year-old Black singer, actor and activist under sustained political persecution, as the APA 2019 and VA/DoD 2022 guidelines and the CMID depression monograph advise: PHQ-9 and GAD-7, a structured diagnostic interview, bipolar screening with the MDQ before an antidepressant, a structured suicide-risk assessment with a safety plan, means counseling and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and tests to exclude medical causes; treating realistic fears of surveillance as realistic rather than as paranoia, and attending to the documented racial disparities in the diagnosis of depression, its treatment and access to ECT; behavioral activation with measurement-based care; adequate trials of an SSRI (sertraline to 200 mg) and an SNRI (venlafaxine to 225 mg), then aripiprazole augmentation for treatment-resistant depression with metabolic monitoring; and an informed consent discussion about modern ECT (general anesthesia, right unilateral ultrabrief pulse, a defined course with cognitive testing) and its alternatives (rTMS and esketamine), decided against for now and kept available. The modern record contrasts careful, consented, measured modern ECT with what is documented about the many treatments he received years later, without asserting the disputed allegations about his care. It is a teaching case, not a claim about his real illness or care.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Robeson returns three days after his first visit and is seen by Dr. Lindqvist-Adebayo of psychiatry today. His blood tests are normal. He still wakes at three in the morning and cannot get back to sleep, has little appetite, and has spent most of the three days at home. On two of the days he again thought he would be better off dead, without any wish or plan to act; he kept to his safety plan, has put his medicines in a locked box, and has the 988 number in his phone. He has had no alcohol. He asked again who can read his record, and the protections were explained. In the structured interview with Dr. Lindqvist-Adebayo he described a first depression about two years ago, after surgery, which lifted slowly over some months without treatment. Before it he had some weeks of intense, absorbed work, sleeping his usual hours, without elation, irritability, racing thoughts or risky behavior.

assessment_plan.display: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe, without psychotic features
assessment_plan.assessment: The structured interview confirms a second major depressive episode, severe, without psychotic features. The MDQ is negative (5 of 13 items, not clustered in one period) and the interview finds no past hypomanic or manic episode: the earlier period of intense work had no reduced need for sleep, elation, irritability or risky behavior. The tests exclude thyroid disease, anemia, low B12 or folate, low testosterone, high calcium, diabetes, HIV and syphilis as causes; he takes no medicine that causes depression. His fear of being watched is realistic for a man in his position and is not a psychotic symptom; recording it as paranoia would repeat a documented pattern of misdiagnosis in Black patients. Dr. Lindqvist-Adebayo and I agree on the plan

Behavioral activation weekly with a psychologist he has chosen
Six-week review; sodium then

hpi.narrative: Mr. Robeson returns six weeks after starting sertraline. He took 50 mg for two weeks with mild nausea that passed in a week, and after the nurse's phone check he has taken 100 mg for three and a half weeks. He has been to five behavioral activation sessions and has begun short walks and an hour of reading each day, but he still wakes early, has little pleasure, and has not sung. He has had no thoughts of being better off dead for three weeks. He has noticed no rise in energy or reduced need for sleep. He takes every dose and keeps his medicines locked.

Options were discussed with him and with Dr. Lindqvist-Adebayo: augmentation with aripiprazole, lithium or a second antidepressant; ECT; rTMS; and esketamine nasal spray. For ECT, informed consent was discussed as a conversation, not a form: it is given under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant and monitoring, usually right unilateral with an ultrabrief pulse to limit memory effects, two or three times a week for a defined course of about six to twelve treatments, with cognitive testing before and during the course; its benefits, risks (anesthesia, headache, muscle aches, and memory loss for events around the course) and alternatives were explained, and he was told he could decline or stop at any time. ECT is not needed now: he has no psychosis, is eating and drinking, and is not suicidal, and he chose augmentation first. Black patients receive ECT less often than white patients with the same diagnosis, so the offer stands on equal terms if augmentation fails. rTMS (daily sessions for about six weeks) and esketamine (twice weekly in the clinic, with blood pressure checks) remain alternatives

assessment.display: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe, without psychotic features
assessment.assessment: He meets criteria for a second major depressive episode, severe, without psychotic features. The MDQ is negative and the interview finds no past hypomanic or manic episode: the earlier period of intense work did not include reduced need for sleep, elation or irritability, so bipolar disorder is not diagnosed, but he should be watched for activation once an antidepressant starts. The tests exclude the common medical causes. Severe depression with a sustained stressor and passive thoughts of death in an older man needs close follow-up, but he has no intent or plan, good supports and a safety plan, so outpatient care is appropriate

His concern about being watched is plausible, specific and consistent with his circumstances; it is not a delusion, and labelling it as paranoia would be a diagnostic error of the kind documented more often in Black patients. Depression, rather than psychosis, explains his presentation, and the persecution is a real stressor that therapy should address directly

recommendations: Outpatient care with the written safety plan, locked medicines, no firearm, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and a C-SSRS screen at every visit; admission if thoughts become active, with intent or a plan
Behavioral activation weekly for about sixteen sessions with a psychologist he chooses, then CBT if needed

Sertraline 50 mg each morning, 100 mg at two weeks, then up to 200 mg by eight weeks as tolerated; sodium at about six weeks; PHQ-9 at every visit, with response as a 50 percent fall and remission as a score below 5

If the PHQ-9 falls by less than a quarter after an adequate trial (at least four to eight weeks at an adequate dose), switch to an SNRI such as venlafaxine extended-release up to 225 mg, with blood pressure checks and 30-day supplies

If a second adequate trial brings only a partial response, treat it as treatment-resistant depression: augmentation with aripiprazole (with metabolic and movement monitoring) or lithium, or ECT, rTMS or esketamine

ECT is not indicated now; it is indicated first for psychotic depression, refusal of food or drink, or acute suicidal risk, and is a choice for treatment-resistant depression. If chosen, it should be given with his own informed consent, under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant, usually right unilateral with an ultrabrief pulse, two or three times a week in a defined course, with the MoCA repeated before and during the course, and with his right to stop at any time
Repeat the MDQ and review the diagnosis if he develops elation, reduced need for sleep or racing thoughts
Explain how his record is protected and keep the psychiatric notes to what care requires

safe_messaging_review.notes: All psychiatric and suicide claims are marked sensitive.
